policy.title: Farming Along a Rising Estuary
policy.opening: The Reed Estuary Land Board must help farming households adapt as rising seas push saltwater onto low fields more often. These households farm side by side, following a traditional planting schedule and sharing farm tasks. The goal is to keep flood-related crop losses low over the next ten years. Engineers expect two plans to meet that goal equally reliably, at the same public cost and with similar household workloads. Higher fields have guaranteed long-term rental agreements, but their scattered locations prevent shared planting and work. Keeping the neighboring fields requires a tidal barrier. Limited land and the barrier’s high starting cost make fully funding both plans unaffordable.
policy.a: The board would rent higher fields for the households and open the low fields to tides, allowing salt marsh to spread. Farmers would adjust to the estuary’s changing edge but lose the neighboring fields that support their shared planting and work traditions.
policy.b: The board would build a tidal barrier around the neighboring fields and support household work teams following the traditional planting schedule. This would preserve farming as a shared way of life, but prevent salt marsh from spreading across those fields as seas rise.

researcher.mechanism_a: Move farming to higher fields with guaranteed long-term rental agreements and allow tides and salt marsh to occupy the low fields, accommodating the changing estuary rather than holding its edge in place.
researcher.mechanism_b: Actively preserve neighboring fields, a traditional planting schedule, and shared farm tasks through a tidal barrier and support for household work teams.
researcher.gain_a: Salt marsh can spread as seas rise, while households continue farming on higher ground.
researcher.gain_b: Households retain the neighboring fields and collective practices that sustain farming as a shared way of life.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Scattered higher fields cannot support the shared planting schedule and work traditions.
researcher.sacrifice_b: The barrier prevents salt marsh from spreading across the protected fields as seas rise.
researcher.shared_goal: Keep flood-related crop losses low for the same farming households.
researcher.expected_success: Engineers expect both plans to meet the crop-loss goal equally reliably.
researcher.costs: The plans have the same public cost and similar household workloads. Limited higher land and the barrier’s high starting cost prevent fully funding both.
researcher.affected_groups: The farming households using the neighboring low fields; the estuary’s fields and potential salt-marsh habitat.
researcher.status_quo_exception: Continuity is central to Option B: new protective works and support for work teams actively preserve the existing planting schedule and shared farm tasks. Option A changes both the farming location and those collective arrangements.
limitations: The barrier could also express Mastery. The intended Embeddedness contrast rests on its explicit purpose of preserving collective farming traditions, not on infrastructure alone.
Scattered fields do not always prevent shared planting and work. This case assumes that their locations prevent those specific practices, not that relocation ends all community ties.
A partial combination might preserve some neighboring fields and allow some marsh expansion, but would not secure both full benefits without sacrifice.

narrative.title: Farming Along a Rising Estuary

The scattered higher fields prevent shared planting and work, breaking up these traditions. Keeping neighboring fields requires a barrier to block tides. Higher fields offer guaranteed long-term rentals, but scattered locations prevent shared planting and work. Limited land and the barrier’s high starting cost prevent fully funding both plans. policy.title: A Changing Community Woodland
policy.opening: The Alder Valley Municipal Woodland Board must reduce fire damage as hotter, drier summers kill trees in a community chestnut grove. Dead wood adds fuel near homes and workshops. Residents share harvest duties and divide chestnuts through a longstanding village agreement. The board owns the grove and can replace failing trees. Its goal is to halve expected fire damage over fifteen years. Local assessments rate both plans equally likely to succeed, with equal public costs and resident workloads. Both remove dead wood and maintain firebreaks. Limited summer water means keeping a productive chestnut grove would leave little room for woodland suited to drier conditions.
policy.a: The board would plant widely spaced, drought-resistant chestnuts and reserve summer water for them. Shared harvest duties and distribution would continue across the village. This would keep the village tradition alive but limit woodland that needs no summer watering.
policy.b: The board would establish dry woodland using locally native trees and shrubs that need no summer watering. Residents would share care duties as the woodland changes. This would fit the drier climate but end the shared chestnut harvest and distribution agreement.

researcher.mechanism_a: The board actively preserves a shared village practice by planting replacement chestnuts, reserving water, and continuing collective harvest duties and distribution.
researcher.mechanism_b: The board replaces the grove with locally native dry woodland. Residents care for trees and shrubs suited to the changing climate rather than maintain a grove that needs summer watering.
researcher.gain_a: Residents retain the collective chestnut harvest and village distribution agreement.
researcher.gain_b: Woodland suited to drier conditions becomes established without summer watering.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Reserving water and space for chestnuts limits woodland that needs no summer watering.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Residents lose the shared chestnut harvest and its distribution agreement.
researcher.shared_goal: Halve expected fire damage near homes and workshops as hotter, drier summers increase dead wood.
researcher.expected_success: Local assessments rate both plans equally likely to halve expected fire damage. Both include dead-wood removal and firebreaks.
researcher.costs: Equal public costs and resident workloads. Summer water is limited; only A reserves it for chestnuts.
researcher.affected_groups: Village residents participating in the shared harvest and distribution, people using nearby homes and workshops, and the community woodland.
researcher.status_quo_exception: Continuity is central to A: active replanting and water allocation preserve a specific existing collective practice. B changes that practice while retaining shared woodland care.
limitations: The distinction is not collective action versus its absence: both plans involve shared duties. It concerns preserving a specific inherited practice versus fitting woodland care to ecological change.
A also involves directing the environment, which can overlap with Mastery. Its intended Embeddedness mechanism is the continued village harvest and distribution arrangement.

A mixed planting might preserve some chestnuts and some dry woodland. The water constraint establishes a trade-off but does not rule out a partial combination; whether that could sustain the village harvest agreement remains uncertain.
Equal fire protection and the suitability of replacement trees are fictional local assessment assumptions, not general claims about chestnut groves or native woodland.

Residents continue sharing harvest duties and dividing chestnuts under their longstanding village agreement. This preserves tradition but leaves little room for woodland needing no summer watering. The goal is to halve expected fire damage over fifteen years. Local assessments rate both available plans equally likely to succeed, with equal public costs and resident workloads.
narrative.b: The Alder Valley Municipal Woodland Board replaces dying chestnuts in its community grove. Hotter, drier summers kill trees, leaving fuel near homes and workshops. The board instead plants locally native trees and shrubs needing no summer watering. Residents share care duties as the woodland changes. This fits the drier climate but ends the longstanding village agreement for shared chestnut harvesting and distribution. The goal is to halve expected fire damage over fifteen years. Local assessments rate both available plans equally likely to succeed, with equal public costs and resident workloads.

policy.title: Winter Recreation With Less Snow
policy.opening: The Bracken Municipal Recreation Board must adapt its hillside recreation ground as warmer winters shorten natural snow cover. Families use this public ground for free winter exercise. Neighborhood teams also practice there for a longstanding ski relay, with older residents teaching children and households sharing preparation duties. The goal is to maintain usable outdoor exercise days over ten winters. Assessments expect both plans to achieve this equally reliably, at equal public and household costs. Cold nights would still allow snowmaking. The narrow hillside cannot hold both a full ski circuit and an undisturbed meadow. Either plan would replace worn facilities, remain free, and provide accessible routes for residents who cannot ski.
policy.a: The board would restore the meadow and build paths around its edge, offering walking or skiing as natural conditions allow. This would accommodate changing snow cover and protect meadow plants, but end the dependable ski season supporting the neighborhood relay and teaching duties.
policy.b: The board would install snowmaking along the ski circuit and organize neighborhood teaching and preparation duties for the annual relay. This would sustain shared winter customs despite declining snowfall, but require water storage and ground leveling that prevent meadow restoration.

researcher.mechanism_a: The board adjusts recreation to natural snow conditions and restores meadow habitat rather than maintaining a fixed ski season.
researcher.mechanism_b: The board actively maintains the annual neighborhood ski relay through snowmaking and organized intergenerational teaching and household preparation duties.
researcher.gain_a: Restored meadow plants and recreation fitted to changing snow conditions.
researcher.gain_b: A dependable ski season supporting shared customs, neighborhood duties, and teaching across generations.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Loss of the dependable ski season that supports the existing relay and its teaching duties.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Water storage and ground leveling prevent meadow restoration.
researcher.shared_goal: Maintain usable outdoor exercise days as warmer winters shorten natural snow cover.
researcher.expected_success: Assessments expect both plans to maintain usable outdoor exercise days equally reliably.
researcher.costs: Equal public and household costs; both replace worn facilities and remain free.
researcher.affected_groups: Families using the public ground, neighborhood relay teams, older residents teaching children, households sharing preparation duties, residents who cannot ski, and meadow plants.
researcher.status_quo_exception: Continuity of the specific ski tradition is central to B. B requires new snowmaking and active organization; it is not inaction. Both options replace existing facilities.
limitations: The contrast concerns accommodation of changing natural conditions versus maintaining a specific collective practice, not nature versus all community activity. A could support new shared walking customs.
A smaller snowmaking area could preserve some skiing alongside some meadow habitat, but would not secure both the full relay circuit and an undisturbed meadow.
Comparable adaptation success depends on the stated assessment that enough cold nights remain for snowmaking over the ten-winter horizon.

policy.title: Playing Fields in Drier Summers
policy.opening: The Brookfield Parks Department must adapt public playing fields to longer summer droughts caused by climate change. Keeping grass green now strains the town’s limited water supply. The department aims to halve water used on these fields over ten years while keeping the same total hours of public sport. Planners expect both options to meet these goals with similar confidence and equal costs. Both replace unrestricted summer bookings. Clubs and casual players use the same fields. The choice concerns when people play and who gets reliable summer access. Some grass can stay green, but there is not enough water for every field.
policy.a: The department would give a council of older residents control over bookings and water schedules. Older players would receive first choice of watered fields. This secures their summer games, but younger players face fewer summer slots and less say.
policy.b: The department would let grass turn brown in summer and recover with seasonal rain. Bookings would follow field conditions, with more games in wetter months. This leaves more water in local streams, but players lose reliable summer games.

researcher.mechanism_a: Age determines who controls bookings and water schedules, and older players receive priority access to watered fields. Authority and access are distributed unequally through age-based roles.
researcher.mechanism_b: The department accommodates seasonal grass growth rather than maintaining green fields throughout drought. Players shift games to wetter months and accept access that follows field conditions.
researcher.gain_a: Older players gain reliable summer games, priority access, and control over schedules.
researcher.gain_b: More water remains in local streams, and field use follows seasonal rain and grass recovery.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Younger players receive fewer summer slots and have less say over shared fields.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Players lose reliable summer games and must move more games to wetter months.
researcher.shared_goal: Halve water used on public playing fields while retaining the same total hours of public sport.
researcher.expected_success: Planners expect both options to meet both goals with similar confidence. B leaves more water in streams as an additional benefit.
researcher.costs: Equal costs. Limited town water prevents keeping every field green through summer.
researcher.affected_groups: Clubs, casual players, older residents, younger players, and local streams.
researcher.status_quo_exception: None. Both replace unrestricted summer bookings.
limitations: Age-based authority and seasonal field management are separable. An older-resident council could oversee seasonal bookings, combining authority with environmental accommodation. That combination would still sacrifice reliable summer access and younger players’ influence.
The hierarchy contrast depends on accepting age as a basis for authority and privileged access, not merely consulting older residents.
Comparable total playing hours assumes enough demand and available daylight in wetter months. The fictional planning estimate includes this assumption.
The options differ in both access rules and seasonal reliability, so responses cannot isolate attitudes toward authority from preferences about summer sport.

policy.title: Sharing Water During Longer Droughts
policy.opening: The Willow Valley Water Board must help farms adapt as climate change brings longer summer droughts. Low river levels leave too little water for all summer crops. The board aims to halve drought-related farm income losses over ten years. Its study expects either plan to meet this goal with similar confidence and equal public costs. Both plans replace emergency water deliveries with planned support for the same farms and workers. Some families inherit seats on a local farming council; these seats currently carry no water rights. The choice concerns which crops receive support and how the board shares scarce summer water.
policy.a: The board would help farms shift planting to rainy months and grow crops that need little summer water. This leaves more water in the river for fish, but farms across the valley must give up some profitable summer crops.
policy.b: The board would give families with inherited council seats first claim on summer water and help other farms switch crops. This secures steady summer harvests on council families’ farms, but leaves less water for fish and less reliable supplies for other farms.

researcher.mechanism_a: Public support shifts farming toward seasonal rain and crops suited to dry summers, accommodating river conditions rather than sustaining summer water demand.
researcher.mechanism_b: Inherited council status determines priority access to scarce summer water. The allocation itself grants an advantage based on inherited rank rather than attaching unrelated authority to a physical project.
researcher.gain_a: More river water remains available for fish.
researcher.gain_b: Council families gain secure summer water and steady summer harvests.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Farms across the valley give up some profitable summer crops.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Less water remains for fish, and farms without inherited council seats receive less reliable water supplies and support to switch crops.
researcher.shared_goal: Halve drought-related farm income losses.
researcher.expected_success: The board's study expects both plans to halve drought-related farm income losses with similar confidence. This is a valley-wide goal, not a promise of equal outcomes for each farm.
researcher.costs: Equal public costs. Longer summer droughts leave insufficient river water for all summer crops.
researcher.affected_groups: The same valley farms and workers, including families with inherited council seats and other farming families; river fish.
researcher.status_quo_exception: None. Both replace emergency deliveries with planned support. Inherited council seats already exist, but priority water rights do not.
limitations: A partial combination is feasible: council families could retain priority while all farms reduce summer planting. It would still trade some secure summer harvests for more river water; it would not fully secure both benefits.

The hierarchy mechanism concerns inherited priority in resource allocation, not technical expertise or an operational need for central control. Respondents may reject the basis of that priority independently of the climate outcome.
Comparable valley-wide income protection is a fictional planning estimate. The distribution of that protection and the amount of water remaining for fish intentionally differ.

researcher.gain_a: Council families gain decision-making power, and their villages gain reliable walking routes.
researcher.gain_b: Hillside plants gain room to recover without walls cutting into wooded slopes.

policy.title: Coastal Protection and Public Recreation
policy.opening: The Bellhaven Coastal Parks Authority must redesign a public waterfront as rising seas let storm waves reach nearby homes and shops more often. Its goal is to reduce flooding over the next twenty years while keeping the waterfront free to enter. Engineers estimate that a raised recreation park and a tidal wetland would provide comparable flood protection, with similar uncertainty. Both would cost the same to build and maintain and protect the same residents and businesses. The narrow site cannot fit both a full protective wetland and broad recreation areas. Either design would replace an existing paved park, changing how visitors use the shore.
policy.a: The authority would build a raised park with flood barriers, skating areas, picnic lawns, and spaces visitors could book for music or games. People could choose varied outdoor pleasures, but barriers would prevent tides from restoring wetland habitat.
policy.b: The authority would restore a tidal wetland, with paths that follow natural channels and close during high tides. Visitors could watch wildlife and experience the changing shore, but would lose space for skating, group games, and music.

researcher.mechanism_b: Public investment restores tidal habitat and arranges paths and access around natural channels and high tides rather than keeping water out of recreation areas.

researcher.gain_b: The shore regains wetland habitat, and visitors can watch wildlife and experience changing tides while nearby homes and shops receive flood protection.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Flood barriers prevent tides from restoring wetland habitat.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Visitors lose space for skating, group games, and music, and paths close during high tides.
researcher.shared_goal: Reduce flooding of nearby homes and shops while keeping the waterfront free to enter.
researcher.expected_success: Engineers estimate comparable flood protection with similar uncertainty for both designs.
researcher.costs: Both designs cost the same to build and maintain. The narrow site cannot accommodate both a full protective wetland and broad recreation areas.
researcher.affected_groups: The same nearby residents and businesses receive protection. Waterfront visitors face different recreation opportunities, and the shoreline faces different habitat outcomes.
limitations: Recreation alone does not establish Affective Autonomy. The intended distinction rests on providing varied spaces for visitors to choose their own enjoyable activities.

policy.title: A Park Lake During Drought
policy.opening: The Alder Valley Parks Department must redesign its public park lake because hotter summers and longer droughts increase evaporation and strain drinking-water supplies. The lake currently needs frequent refilling with drinking water. The department aims to cut that use by at least three quarters over ten years while keeping the site free to enter. Planners expect both designs to meet this goal with similar reliability and equal building and maintenance costs. Both serve the same nearby neighborhoods and replace the existing ornamental lake. The main decision concerns water levels: allowing seasonal drying or maintaining steady water for recreation within a tighter water budget.
policy.a: The department would reshape the lake into a seasonal wetland fed by rain and runoff. Paths would follow its changing edges, giving native plants and wildlife room to return. Visitors could observe seasonal changes but would lose reliable open-water recreation.
policy.b: The department would line the lake and treat recycled water to maintain steady levels for free paddleboarding and floating play areas. Visitors could choose varied water activities throughout summer, but the fixed shoreline would leave little room for seasonal wetland habitat.

narrative.title: Recreation During Hotter Summers
narrative.a: Linden’s Municipal Recreation Department replaces aging hillside courts as climate change makes summer afternoons too hot for outdoor programs. Level space is scarce. The department clears much of the wooded slope to build a solar-powered, cooled center, removing woodland and wildlife habitat. Residents follow accessible paths to free dance, games, and climbing throughout the day. They choose varied activities on flexible schedules. Planners compare the center with shaded outdoor programs scheduled for cooler mornings and evenings. They expect either option to restore the same number of comfortable summer recreation hours over the next ten years, equally reliably. Both options serve the same residents and have equal construction and operating costs.
narrative.b: Linden’s Municipal Recreation Department replaces aging hillside courts as climate change makes summer afternoons too hot for outdoor programs. Level space is scarce; a large indoor center requires clearing much of the wooded slope. The department fits shaded outdoor spaces around existing trees. Residents follow accessible paths to free programs held on cooler mornings and evenings, away from wildlife nesting areas. They gain woodland experiences but lose daytime flexibility and activities needing enclosed rooms. Planners expect these spaces and a cooled center to restore the same number of comfortable summer recreation hours over the next ten years, equally reliably. Both options serve the same residents and have equal construction and operating costs.

A explicitly identifies shaded outdoor programs as the option planners compare with the center, not as an additional part of the center’s program.

The inferred Schwartz cultural orientation contrast is Affective Autonomy in A, expressed through varied enjoyable activities and flexible schedules, versus Harmony in B, expressed through fitting programs around trees, cooler hours, and wildlife nesting areas. The source provides no intended value labels, so this interpretation remains tentative.

The source does not establish whether a smaller indoor facility combined with outdoor spaces could retain both benefits. The space constraint supports the stated trade-off for a large center but does not rule out mixed designs. The stories preserve rather than resolve this limitation.

policy.title: Growing Through Hotter Summers
policy.opening: The Larkfield Municipal Garden Service must adapt its public food gardens as climate change brings hotter, drier summers. Water limits now threaten harvests for plot holders across the district. The service can fund one redesign, with equal spending and access to plots under either plan. Both plans are expected to maintain roughly today's annual food harvests over the next ten years while using less water, with similar confidence. Most food would grow in cooler months. The main choice concerns summer use of the limited garden space: leaving connected areas undisturbed for local wildlife or making that space available for independent growing experiments.
policy.a: The service would shape planting around local seasonal cycles, leaving connected summer areas for drought-adapted plants and wildlife. Gardeners would gain space that follows natural rhythms but accept planting limits that rule out their own summer growing experiments.
policy.b: The service would let gardeners develop and test their own summer growing ideas within equal water allowances, using movable shade and stored rainwater. Gardeners would gain freedom to investigate different approaches but leave less connected, undisturbed summer habitat.

researcher.mechanism_a: The public garden redesign accommodates local seasonal cycles and reserves connected summer areas for drought-adapted plants and wildlife, limiting cultivation during the dry season.
researcher.mechanism_b: The public garden redesign gives gardeners room to develop and test their own growing ideas within equal water allowances.
researcher.gain_a: Connected, undisturbed summer habitat and a growing schedule fitted to local natural rhythms.
researcher.gain_b: Freedom for gardeners to choose and investigate different summer growing approaches.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Planting limits rule out gardeners' independent summer growing experiments.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Summer experiments leave less connected, undisturbed habitat for local plants and wildlife.
researcher.shared_goal: Adapt public food gardens to hotter, drier summers while maintaining annual food harvests and using less water.
researcher.expected_success: Both plans are expected to maintain roughly today's annual food harvests while using less water, with similar confidence.
researcher.costs: Equal public spending; equal access to plots under either plan.
researcher.affected_groups: Public garden plot holders across the district and local plants and wildlife using the gardens.
researcher.status_quo_exception: None. Both alternatives introduce a funded garden redesign.
limitations: Independent growing experiments also involve some direction of the natural environment. Option B expresses Intellectual Autonomy primarily through gardeners choosing and testing their own ideas, rather than through control of nature itself.

A partial combination could preserve some habitat and permit some experiments. Limited garden space means that expanding summer experiments would still reduce the connected area left undisturbed; combining the plans would not fully secure both benefits.
The contrast concerns independent summer experiments, not freedom of inquiry in every season.

policy.title: Redesigning a Floodplain Park
policy.opening: The Bellwater Parks Authority must redesign a riverside park as climate change brings heavier rain and more frequent river floods. Nearby homes need protection, and residents need continued access to outdoor space. The park has limited room to hold floodwater between the river and homes. Two new layouts would cost the same and are expected, with similar confidence, to reduce flooding of nearby homes equally over twenty years. Both retain accessible paths and the same total public space. The choice concerns whether residents can test their own park designs or whether connected channels let seasonal river flows shape the park.
policy.a: The authority would fund residents to test their own ideas for paths, planting, and wet areas. Each test must leave enough room for floodwater. Residents could explore different designs, but dividing the park into test areas would break up connected river habitat.
policy.b: The authority would restore connected channels and let seasonal floods shape the park’s plants and wet areas. Residents would gain a landscape that follows river flows, but rules protecting those connections would limit which park designs they could test.

researcher.mechanism_a: Public funding lets residents test their own ideas for paths, planting, and wet areas, provided they leave enough room for floodwater.
researcher.mechanism_b: The authority restores connected channels and lets seasonal floods shape the landscape. Rules restrict tests that would disrupt those connections.
researcher.gain_a: Residents gain funded opportunities to explore their own park designs.
researcher.gain_b: Residents gain connected river habitat and a landscape shaped by seasonal river flows.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Dividing the park into test areas breaks up connected river habitat.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Residents face limits on which park designs they can test.
researcher.shared_goal: Adapt to heavier rain and more frequent river floods by holding floodwater in the park and reducing flooding of nearby homes.
researcher.expected_success: Both layouts are expected to reduce flooding of nearby homes equally, with similar confidence.
researcher.costs: Both layouts cost the same, retain accessible paths, and provide the same total public space.
researcher.affected_groups: Residents of nearby homes, park users, residents interested in testing designs, and river habitat.
limitations: Resident-designed tests could also follow river flows. The contrast concerns freedom to test different layouts versus protecting connected seasonal flow routes, not experimentation versus environmental concern.
Some tests could fit within the connected-channel layout. A combined plan could preserve some opportunities to explore ideas, although tests that break protected connections would remain restricted.

policy.title: Adapting a Reservoir Forest
policy.opening: The Alder Basin Water Authority must manage its reservoir forest as hotter, drier summers increase severe wildfire risk. Fires that strip hillsides can wash ash and soil into the reservoir, disrupting water service for nearby towns. The authority can treat only the forest it owns, and steep slopes limit access. Two plans cost the same. Planners expect both to reduce fire-related water disruptions equally over fifteen years. Both estimates carry similar uncertainty. Both plans use careful thinning and controlled fires. The choice concerns how the treated forest develops: connected areas shaped by natural recovery or separate plots where local research teams pursue their own questions.
policy.a: The authority would maintain connected areas where controlled fires and natural seed growth shape forest recovery. This would support movement of native plants and wildlife, but rules against dividing these areas would restrict research teams’ independent experiments.
policy.b: The authority would offer local research teams equal access to plots for testing their own forest recovery ideas within fire-safety limits. Teams could pursue different questions, but patches with different planting and cutting would break up the naturally recovering forest.

researcher.mechanism_a: The authority organizes forest treatment around connected natural recovery, using controlled fire and natural seed growth while limiting experiments that divide those areas.
researcher.mechanism_b: The authority provides equal access to plots where local research teams choose their own questions and test different recovery ideas within common fire-safety limits.
researcher.gain_a: Connected natural recovery supports movement of native plants and wildlife.
researcher.gain_b: Local research teams gain room to pursue independent questions and different forest recovery ideas.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Rules protecting connected recovery areas restrict independent experiments.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Experimental patches with different planting and cutting break up the naturally recovering forest.
researcher.shared_goal: Reduce wildfire-related ash and soil entering the reservoir and disrupting nearby towns’ water service as summers become hotter and drier.
researcher.expected_success: Planners expect equal reductions in fire-related water disruptions. Both estimates carry similar uncertainty.
researcher.costs: Both plans cost the same. Both face limited publicly owned treatment land and restricted access on steep slopes.
researcher.affected_groups: Nearby towns using reservoir water, local research teams, and native forest plants and wildlife.
limitations: Harmony here requires active forest management; controlled fire and thinning express accommodation only because connected natural recovery guides their use.
Independent experiments may also express Mastery. The intended distinction is teams choosing their own intellectual questions, not achieving greater control or better water-service outcomes.
Some independent research could occur without dividing recovery areas. The tradeoff applies to experiments requiring separate treatments, not to observation or every form of inquiry.

policy.title: Housing Above Rising Coastal Waters
policy.opening: The Bracken Bay Housing Authority must protect a housing estate from flooding as climate change raises sea levels. Tenants share courtyard meals, gardening, and rotating care duties. policy.title: Recreation During Hotter Summers
policy.opening: The Bellwater Parks Department must adapt neighborhood recreation centers as climate change brings hotter summers. Heat increasingly interrupts outdoor games, dancing, and informal leisure for residents of all ages. The department wants to restore the lost hours of comfortable summer recreation over the next ten years. Centers currently host both neighborhood traditions and individually chosen activities. A fixed building and staffing budget limits how much space can stay comfortable and supervised. Two proposed programs cost the same and are expected to restore similar recreation hours, with similar confidence. Both offer free access, step-free facilities, and equipment, but organize summer recreation differently.
policy.a: The department would shade courtyards and staff cooler evening sessions built around neighborhood dances and games taught across generations. Shared schedules would sustain these practices and regular group participation, but leave fewer comfortable spaces for residents seeking different activities or times.
policy.b: The department would cool indoor rooms and staff flexible sessions where residents choose among music, games, dance, and quiet relaxation. This would support varied personal enjoyment, but leave fewer comfortable spaces reserved for neighborhood traditions and regular whole-group gatherings.

researcher.mechanism_b: Public investment organizes comfortable recreation around flexible sessions and individually chosen enjoyable activities.

researcher.gain_b: Residents gain flexible opportunities to choose varied enjoyable experiences for themselves.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Residents seeking different activities or times have fewer comfortable spaces available.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Neighborhood traditions and regular whole-group gatherings have fewer dedicated comfortable spaces.
researcher.shared_goal: Restore summer recreation hours lost to increasing heat.
researcher.expected_success: Both programs are expected to restore similar hours of comfortable summer recreation, with similar confidence.
researcher.costs: The programs cost the same within a fixed building and staffing budget. Both provide free access, step-free facilities, and equipment.
researcher.affected_groups: Residents of all ages using neighborhood recreation centers, including participants in shared traditions and individually chosen activities.
researcher.status_quo_exception: Both are new adaptation programs. A intentionally sustains existing neighborhood practices through new shading and staffed evening sessions; continuity is part of the intended contrast, not inaction. The baseline includes both traditional and individually chosen recreation.
limitations: Shared dancing and games can also provide personal enjoyment. The distinction concerns how public space and schedules support shared practices versus individual choice, not whether participants enjoy themselves.

A mixed program is feasible, but the fixed building and staffing budget means dividing resources would reduce the dedicated capacity available for each benefit. The alternatives represent priorities rather than technically exclusive designs.
Comparable recreation hours do not imply that residents value evening outdoor sessions and flexible indoor sessions equally.

The service plans to halve meal-related emissions over five years while keeping meals affordable and nourishing for residents of all ages. policy.title: Designing a Coastal Relocation
policy.opening: The Northhaven Municipal Housing Authority must relocate a coastal neighborhood because rising seas increasingly flood its homes. Its 180 households currently share courtyards used for communal meals, seasonal gatherings, and passing on local crafts. The authority aims to keep all households beyond projected flood reach for the next 30 years. Two plans offer equally reliable protection, equal home sizes, and the same moving date and public cost. Both give every household a replacement home. The inland site has limited space: connected communal courtyards require coordinated house layouts, while allowing households to develop independent layouts leaves less room for those shared spaces.
policy.a: The authority would have households and longtime craft groups develop a coordinated layout around shared courtyards. This would carry communal meals, gatherings, and teaching into the new neighborhood, but households would accept common design rules rather than pursue independent layouts.
policy.b: The authority would give each household design support to investigate and develop its own layout within equal space allowances. This would support independent ideas about coastal living, but smaller, scattered shared spaces would limit neighborhood-wide gatherings and craft teaching.

researcher.gain_b: Households can independently investigate and develop layouts suited to their own ideas about coastal living.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Households accept common design rules and forgo independent layouts.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Smaller, scattered shared spaces limit neighborhood-wide gatherings and craft teaching.
researcher.shared_goal: Relocate all 180 households beyond projected coastal flood reach.
researcher.expected_success: Both plans offer equally reliable protection from projected flooding, with a replacement home of equal size for every household.

researcher.costs: The same public cost; both plans provide equal home sizes.
researcher.affected_groups: The same 180 coastal households, including participants in communal gatherings and local craft groups.

policy.title: Sharing a Warmer Village Hall

policy.title: Changing Neighborhood Meal Menus
policy.opening: The Riverton Municipal Meals Service plans to cut climate pollution from meat-heavy menus at its neighborhood dining rooms. Producing beef and lamb releases gases that warm the climate. The rooms serve longtime residents and newcomers, and hold weekly meals tied to a longstanding seasonal calendar. The goal is to cut food-related emissions by about one-third within three years. Two menu plans offer comparable cuts, with similar uncertainty, costs, nutrition, and opening hours. Both meet medical dietary needs. Small kitchens can prepare only one main dish per sitting, apart from medical alternatives. policy.b: The service would give all diners equal votes on rotating menus, with volunteers helping groups negotiate fair turns for their preferred dishes. This would spread influence and the burden of adapting, but replace some established seasonal meals with newly chosen ones.

policy.title: Preparing Orchards for Drier Summers
policy.opening: The Millbrook Orchard Board must reduce water used on its public fruit farms as climate change brings longer summer droughts. Local households lease the farms and sell their harvests. The reservoir cannot supply current watering needs during dry years. Many trees also need replacing, so the board can change planting layouts or install pipes that deliver water directly to roots. Both plans cost the same, including upkeep, and cover the same households. Farm advisers expect either to cut water use by about one-quarter over ten years, with similar confidence. Both maintain total fruit production and household earnings. The board must also assign control over farm work.
policy.a: The board would empower farm crews to remove plot boundaries, reshape rows, and replace mixed trees with one productive variety. Crews could direct planting across all farms. This makes machine harvesting easier, but households lose fruit varieties and separate plots.
policy.b: The board would install root-watering pipes. Households whose farm leases passed down through their families would control watering on everyone's plots. Separate plots and mixed fruit harvests remain, but farms need more hand harvesting and newer households have less control.

researcher.mechanism_a: Farm crews receive authority to reshape the farms across plot boundaries and standardize planting for productive, machine-friendly orchards. The expression rests on active transformation and direction, not machinery alone.
researcher.mechanism_b: Households whose farm leases passed down through their families receive control over watering on everyone's plots. Unequal authority follows inherited position rather than demonstrated performance.
researcher.gain_a: Crews can direct planting across the farms, and the new rows and single variety make machine harvesting easier.
researcher.gain_b: Households keep separate plots and mixed fruit harvests. Households with inherited leases gain authority over watering.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Households lose separate plots and fruit varieties.
researcher.sacrifice_b: The farms require more hand harvesting, and newer households have less control over watering.
researcher.shared_goal: Reduce orchard water use during longer summer droughts while maintaining total fruit production and household earnings.
researcher.expected_success: Farm advisers expect both plans to cut water use by about one-quarter, with similar confidence, while maintaining total production and household earnings.
researcher.costs: Both plans cost the same, including upkeep. B requires more hand harvesting; A makes machine harvesting easier.
researcher.affected_groups: The same households leasing public fruit farms, including households with inherited leases and newer households, and the farm crews.
researcher.status_quo_exception: B preserves separate plots and mixed fruit, but introduces pipes and assigns leadership based on inherited leases. Continuity is a practical consequence, not the evidence for Hierarchy.
limitations: The physical and governance choices are not inseparable. Pipes could be installed without authority based on inherited leases, and households with inherited leases could oversee redesigned orchards. This bundled contrast therefore cannot isolate the value pair cleanly.
A combines several water-saving changes. Their expected effectiveness and the comparable costs and earnings are fictional planning assumptions, not claims about all orchards.
B's preservation of plots and fruit varieties is not itself evidence of Hierarchy; inherited status granting control over other households' watering supplies that evidence.

policy.title: Heating a Public Art School
policy.opening: The Brookside Municipal Art School must cut emissions from gas heating that contributes to climate change. Its old heating system warms whole wings, even when few rooms are used. The school cannot afford a new heating system, but can change rooms and schedules. Keeping private studios means opening fewer hours to meet the heating limit. Shared studios would fit everyone into fewer heated wings, allowing longer hours. Both plans serve the same teachers and students and cost the same. Building advisers expect either to cut heating emissions by about one-third over five years, with similar confidence. The school must choose how to organize the space.
policy.a: The school would give teachers holding senior posts private studios and authority over room assignments. Junior teachers would share rooms and follow their decisions. Senior teachers gain quiet working space, but everyone faces shorter opening hours.
policy.b: The school would replace private studios with shared workrooms. Staff teams would compete to achieve the longest opening hours within the heating limit, repeatedly redesigning layouts and schedules to beat their own records. Everyone gains longer access, but teachers lose private space.

researcher.mechanism_a: Institutional rank determines unequal space and power. Teachers holding senior posts receive private studios and authority over room assignments. Junior teachers share rooms and follow their decisions.
researcher.mechanism_b: The school organizes staff teams around competitive achievement. Teams actively reshape layouts and schedules to outperform one another and beat their own access records while meeting the heating limit.
researcher.gain_a: Senior teachers gain quiet private studios and authority over room assignments.
researcher.gain_b: Teachers and students gain longer studio access. Teams pursue measurable success through competition and repeated improvements to room use and schedules.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Everyone faces shorter opening hours. Junior teachers share rooms and follow senior teachers' room decisions.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Teachers lose private working space. Staff teams must repeatedly redesign arrangements and compete over the opening hours they achieve.
researcher.shared_goal: Cut emissions from the public art school's gas heating.
researcher.expected_success: Building advisers expect either plan to cut heating emissions by about one-third, with similar confidence.
researcher.costs: Both plans cost the same. A new heating system is unaffordable. Keeping private studios requires shorter opening hours; shared studios allow longer hours by concentrating activity in fewer heated wings.
researcher.affected_groups: The same students and teachers, including teachers holding senior posts and junior teachers. B organizes staff into competing teams.
researcher.status_quo_exception: None. A retains private studios but introduces rank-based allocation and room authority alongside shorter hours. B replaces private studios and introduces competition over extending access.
limitations: Hierarchy and Mastery can coexist. Senior teachers could direct shared studios while teams compete to improve access. That combination would still sacrifice A's private-space benefit under the stated heating constraint.

Competition and record-breaking strengthen B's emphasis on achievement and active control, but are not technically necessary to operate shared studios. Respondents may judge competition itself rather than the broader orientation.

Longer access benefits everyone, so B may still suggest Egalitarianism. Its intended distinguishing mechanism is competitive achievement through repeatedly reshaping working arrangements, not equal decision power or voluntary mutual help.
A expresses Hierarchy through institutional rank rather than inherited status. B remains a narrow school-management example and may still be read partly as practical efficiency.

policy.opening: The Northbridge Public University must cut emissions from research flights, which add heat-trapping gases to the atmosphere. Researchers could pursue independent ideas, but large coordinated studies would lose priority and depend on researchers choosing to combine their allowances.

policy.title: Planning Forest Fire Treatments
policy.opening: The Redstone Regional Forest Service must protect public woodlands as hotter summers dry fallen branches and help wildfires spread. The programs differ in who controls treatment plans and how much planning time they need.

researcher.mechanism_b: Senior officers receive larger test plots and final authority because of institutional rank. Junior foresters work within the officers' connected plan.

researcher.gain_b: Rank-based control supports one connected treatment plan and leaves more crew time for routine trail upkeep.

researcher.sacrifice_b: Junior foresters cannot independently test competing treatment ideas.

researcher.costs: Equal budgets. Limited crew time must cover brush removal, burn planning, and routine trail upkeep. Option A uses more time for planning; Option B leaves more time for trail upkeep.
researcher.affected_groups: The same nearby residents, forest workers, and visitors, including senior officers and junior foresters.

policy.title: Sharing Water During Longer Droughts

policy.b: The board would give every grower an equal vote on a council that shares responsibility for water limits. Preferred delivery times would rotate among farms. Small growers would gain equal access, while estate schedules would become less predictable.

policy.title: Public Meals Under Drought
policy.opening: The Dunmere Municipal Meals Service must adapt its public cafeterias to longer droughts that disrupt crop supplies. It serves workers, students, and older residents. policy.a: The service would contract an indoor farm to control growing conditions and deliver fixed crops throughout the year. Production targets would rise as growers refine their methods. Diners would gain predictable meals despite drought, but have a narrower range of flavors.
policy.b: The service would buy drought-tolerant seasonal crops from several regions and let diners choose among changing dishes, tastings, and spice combinations. Diners would gain varied, enjoyable meals, but favorite dishes would sometimes disappear as harvests and available ingredients change.

policy.title: Winter Tourism With Less Snow
policy.opening: The Alder Ridge Mountain Recreation Authority must adapt its public winter resort to warmer winters that shorten natural snow cover. Local workers and visiting households depend on its affordable winter season. Its goal is to maintain winter visitor days over the next ten years. Planners expect two proposals to achieve this equally well, with similar uncertainty. Both have equal public costs, ticket prices, and low emissions from clean electricity. Neither changes nearby drinking-water supplies. The resort must replace its aging lifts and trails. Its capital budget can support either a varied, mostly snow-free resort or a compact snowmaking system, but not both complete networks.

Staff would pursue increasingly reliable snow coverage through testing and strict operating targets. Visitors would gain dependable skiing, but lose most other recreation choices.

policy.title: Designing Lower-Methane Rice Farming
policy.opening: The Bellwater Public Agricultural Institute manages a rice-growing district where flooded soils release methane, a gas that warms the climate. It plans a five-year program to cut methane while maintaining rice harvests for the same growers. Its budget covers new water gates, field equipment, and paid time for growers to participate. Two approaches have equal costs and are expected to cut methane by about one-third, with similar uncertainty and unchanged average harvests. Coordinating water levels across fields allows tighter control, but leaves less room for independent experiments. Separate field schedules allow growers to test different ideas, but prevent district-wide control of growing conditions.
policy.a: The institute would equip growers to run a coordinated system that adjusts field water levels to control methane and growing conditions. This would make harvest dates more predictable, but growers would follow a shared experimental plan rather than pursue their own questions.
policy.b: The institute would give grower teams equipment and freedom to design separate methane-reduction trials, within tested limits that protect harvests. Teams could investigate their own questions about water timing and soil treatments, but harvest dates would remain less predictable.

researcher.mechanism_b: The institute distributes equipment and protects grower teams' freedom to choose questions and design separate climate-related experiments.

researcher.gain_b: Grower teams can pursue their own ideas about reducing methane through water timing and soil treatments.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Growers must follow a shared experimental plan instead of pursuing their own questions.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Separate experiments give up district-wide control and leave harvest dates less predictable.
researcher.shared_goal: Reduce methane from rice farming while maintaining average rice harvests.
researcher.expected_success: Both approaches are expected to reduce methane by about one-third, with similar uncertainty and unchanged average harvests.
researcher.costs: Equal program costs covering water gates, field equipment, and paid grower participation.
researcher.affected_groups: The same rice growers in the institute-managed district.

policy.title: Allocating Water During Longer Droughts
policy.opening: The Redvale Water District must reduce water used on crops as climate change brings longer droughts. Less water now reaches its reservoir. It serves forty equal-sized vegetable farms facing similar water shortages. Its goal is to cut annual farm water use by one quarter within five years. Trials suggest two plans would achieve this with similar confidence and equal public and farmer costs. Both replace current water contracts and provide equipment and training. One tightly controls growing conditions to increase harvests; the other shares water and decisions equally. With a fixed water supply, equal shares leave less water for farms that can produce the largest harvests.
policy.a: The district would give more water to farms that can grow more vegetables, using sensors and controlled growing beds to direct moisture precisely. This increases total harvests and control over growing conditions, but leaves some farms with less water and smaller harvests.
policy.b: The district would give each farm an equal water share and an equal vote in scheduling deliveries. Farmers would jointly arrange planting reductions to stay within the limit. This spreads losses evenly, but produces fewer vegetables overall.

researcher.mechanism_b: Equal-sized farms receive equal water shares and equal voting power, and farmers jointly arrange planting reductions to spread losses evenly.

researcher.gain_b: Equal access to water, equal influence over delivery schedules, and evenly spread harvest losses.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Some farms receive less water and have smaller harvests.
researcher.sacrifice_b: The district produces fewer vegetables overall than under the plan that directs water toward larger harvests.
researcher.shared_goal: Reduce annual water used on crops by one quarter to adapt to longer droughts and less water reaching the reservoir.
researcher.expected_success: Trials suggest both plans would achieve the same water-use reduction with similar confidence.
researcher.costs: Equal public and farmer costs; both plans provide equipment and training.
researcher.affected_groups: Forty equal-sized vegetable farms facing similar water shortages.
researcher.status_quo_exception: None. Both options replace current water contracts.
limitations: Mastery is expressed through the collective pursuit of larger harvests and control over growing conditions, not through sensors alone.

Equal shares could be combined with precise growing controls, but this would not remove the stated allocation trade-off: it would still leave less water for farms capable of producing the largest harvests.

policy.title: Sharing Loading Space for Cleaner Deliveries
policy.opening: The Bellhaven Transport Authority must cut greenhouse gases from diesel deliveries to shops and homes. Forty small delivery firms serve one district, where scarce loading bays cause queues and wasted fuel. The goal is to halve delivery emissions within six years without reducing goods delivered. Both plans provide electric vans and shared equipment for combining loads. Trials suggest both would meet the goal with similar confidence. Public costs and total business costs would be the same. Firms handle different goods, so some can unload faster than others. Giving firms equal access to busy morning slots spreads this benefit but limits how much the authority can speed up deliveries.
policy.a: The authority would establish a cooperative with equal votes. Firms would voluntarily combine loads and share morning slots equally, helping each other cover difficult routes. This spreads access and responsibility evenly, but customers wait longer for deliveries than under Policy B.
policy.b: The authority would set demanding delivery targets and continually adjust routes and loading schedules to beat previous times. Firms moving more goods per slot would earn more morning access. Deliveries become faster, but slower firms receive fewer convenient slots.

researcher.mechanism_a: Equal votes, voluntary load sharing, equal morning access, and mutual help on difficult routes organize firms around shared responsibility and equal standing.
researcher.mechanism_b: The authority actively reshapes routes and schedules around demanding performance targets. Firms earn scarce morning access by moving more goods per slot.
researcher.gain_a: Firms share convenient loading access, decisions, and responsibility evenly.
researcher.gain_b: Continual adjustment and performance-based access make deliveries faster.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Customers wait longer for deliveries than under Policy B.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Slower firms receive fewer convenient morning slots, including firms whose goods take longer to unload.
researcher.shared_goal: Halve greenhouse gas emissions from district deliveries without reducing goods delivered.
researcher.expected_success: Trials suggest both plans would meet the emissions goal with similar confidence.
researcher.costs: The plans have equal public costs and equal total business costs. Both provide electric vans and shared equipment for combining loads; equal total costs do not imply equal access for each firm.
researcher.affected_groups: Forty small delivery firms in one district and the shops and households receiving their deliveries.
limitations: Equal governance can coexist with demanding targets and route adjustment. The distinction rests on equal access and mutual responsibility versus allocating scarce morning access to improve measured performance, not on cooperation versus technology.
A mixed plan could retain some equal access while improving speed. It cannot give every firm equal morning access and also give faster firms more of those same scarce slots.
Mastery remains close to ordinary operational efficiency here. Continually surpassing previous delivery times and rewarding demonstrated performance carry the intended distinction.

policy.title: Designing a Summer Cooling Center
policy.opening: The Bellwater Municipal Buildings Department plans to convert an empty depot into a free cooling center as climate change brings longer, hotter summers. Many nearby apartment residents lack cooling and lose comfortable daytime hours at home. The goal is to give these residents usable indoor space during heatwaves over the next five summers. The budget covers cooling and fitting out the depot, but its floor area limits the activities it can support. Both designs cost the same, offer the same opening hours, and are expected to provide equally reliable cooling for the same number of visitors. Participation in activities would be optional. Neither design would displace an existing service.
policy.a: The department would equip the center for visitors to choose music, games, and recreational activities independently. Residents would gain varied ways to enjoy hot days, but sound and floor-space needs would leave little room for sustained individual study or creative projects.
policy.b: The department would equip the center with quiet work areas, research materials, and project benches that visitors could use to pursue their own questions and ideas. Residents would gain space for independent exploration, but quiet rules would restrict lively recreation.

researcher.gain_b: Residents gain conditions and resources for sustained, self-directed inquiry and creative work during hot days.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Noise and floor-space demands leave little room for sustained individual study or creative projects.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Quiet rules restrict lively recreation.
researcher.shared_goal: Provide nearby apartment residents who lack cooling with usable indoor space during increasingly long, hot summers.
researcher.expected_success: Both designs are expected to provide equally reliable cooling for the same number of visitors, with identical opening hours.
researcher.costs: Both designs cost the same within a budget covering cooling and fitting out the depot. Limited floor area constrains the activities offered.
researcher.affected_groups: Nearby apartment residents who lack cooling; access is free and participation in activities is optional under either design.
limitations: Enjoyment and independent exploration can overlap: games may stimulate inquiry, and creative projects may be pleasurable. The distinction rests on which activities the public space deliberately supports.

policy.title: Cutting Emissions From Rice Fields
policy.opening: The Fenvale Agricultural Water Board must reduce methane from flooded rice fields, where rotting plant matter releases this warming gas. It can fund new watering schedules that let fields dry briefly without harming crops. Forty farms share its canals, but each has a separate water gate. The five-year program has limited funding for field advisers and paid farm help during busy planting weeks. Two plans cost the same and cover all forty farms. Trials suggest both would cut methane by about one-quarter while maintaining total harvests, with similar confidence. The board must decide how to divide support between shared assistance and farmer-led experiments.
policy.a: The board would give farmers equal votes over a shared watering plan and pool paid help for farms with fewer workers. Farmers would cooperate to spread the extra workload fairly, but could not fund separate experiments outside their agreed plan.
policy.b: The board would give each farmer an equal adviser allowance to test and refine a watering schedule independently. Farmers could pursue their own questions, but less funding would remain for pooled help, leaving farms with fewer workers carrying heavier workloads.

researcher.mechanism_a: Farmers have equal votes and cooperate to allocate paid help according to staffing needs, sharing the added work more fairly.
researcher.mechanism_b: Each farmer receives adviser support to investigate personal questions and independently develop and test a watering schedule.
researcher.gain_a: Farms with fewer workers receive pooled assistance, spreading the extra workload more fairly.
researcher.gain_b: Farmers gain room to pursue independent questions and refine their own watering ideas.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Public support does not cover separate experiments outside the shared plan.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Less pooled help remains, so farms with fewer workers carry heavier workloads.
researcher.shared_goal: Reduce methane released by flooded rice fields while maintaining total harvests.
researcher.expected_success: Trials suggest both plans would reduce methane by about one-quarter and maintain total harvests, with similar confidence.
researcher.costs: Both plans cost the same. Limited funding covers field advisers and paid farm help during busy planting weeks; spending more on independent experiments leaves less for shared assistance.
researcher.affected_groups: Forty rice farms sharing canals, including farms with fewer workers. Each farm has a separate water gate.
limitations: A mixed plan could retain some independent experiments and some pooled assistance, but the fixed support budget would require sacrificing part of each benefit.

Equal adviser allowances in B also express equal access. The intended distinction is independent inquiry versus cooperative allocation of help according to need, not equality versus its complete absence.
Comparable emissions reductions and total harvests are fictional trial-based assumptions; they do not imply equal workloads across farms.

narrative.title: Cutting Emissions From Rice Fields

Forty farms share canals but have separate gates. Five-year funding limits advisers and paid help during busy planting weeks. Farmers use equal votes to agree on watering schedules and pool paid help for farms with fewer workers. They share the extra workload fairly but cannot fund experiments outside their agreed plan. Both available approaches cost the same and cover all forty farms. Trials suggest, with similar confidence, that either cuts methane by about one-quarter while maintaining total harvests. Brief drying is not expected to harm crops.
narrative.b: The Fenvale Agricultural Water Board funds brief drying of rice fields to cut methane, a warming gas released by rotting plants in flooded fields. Forty farms share canals but have separate gates. Five-year funding limits advisers and paid help during busy planting weeks. Each farmer receives an equal adviser allowance to test and refine watering schedules independently. Farmers pursue their own questions, but less funding remains for pooled help, leaving farms with fewer workers carrying heavier workloads. Both available approaches cost the same and cover all forty farms. Trials suggest, with similar confidence, that either cuts methane by about one-quarter while maintaining total harvests. Brief drying is not expected to harm crops.
adaptation_notes: Scenario A contains 110 words; Scenario B contains 112 words. Both use present-tense hypothetical accounts and preserve trial-based uncertainty.
The source supplies no numerical cost estimate. Both stories retain its same-cost comparison without adding costs or precision.

The source provides no intended cultural value labels. A's equal voting and fair sharing of labor suggest Egalitarianism; B's independent questioning and experiments suggest Intellectual Autonomy. This distinction is imperfect: B also distributes adviser support equally, and cooperation alone does not establish Embeddedness.

Limited funding creates the stated trade-off between shared assistance and independent experiments. The source does not establish whether a mixed allocation could retain both benefits; the narratives preserve its alternatives rather than inventing restrictions to rule out a combination.

policy.title: Changing School Lunch Recipes
policy.opening: The Dunmere School Meals Service plans to cut climate pollution from lunches because raising cattle releases methane, a heat-trapping gas. It serves twelve schools whose kitchens have different staffing levels. The goal is to replace half the beef served with nutritious bean-based meals over three years. Meal trials suggest students would accept either plan equally well. Evaluators expect both to meet the goal with similar confidence. Both serve the same students, involve the same workers, cost the same, and protect meal quality. A limited staff budget must cover time for cooks to test their own recipes or help kitchens prepare meals. Neither activity currently receives dedicated funding.
policy.a: The service would give each kitchen paid time for cooks to investigate their own recipe ideas without group approval. This would support independent learning and distinct menus, but leave less help for understaffed kitchens, where preparing beans would add more work per cook.
policy.b: The service would let kitchen workers agree on recipes through equal votes and pool paid preparation help according to staffing needs. This would spread added work more evenly, but cooks would lose funded time to explore ideas outside the shared menu.

researcher.mechanism_a: Public funding gives cooks protected time to investigate recipe ideas independently, without needing group approval.
researcher.mechanism_b: Workers have equal votes over recipes and cooperate by directing pooled preparation help toward understaffed kitchens.
researcher.gain_a: Independent learning and distinct menus developed through cooks' own investigations.
researcher.gain_b: A more even distribution of added preparation work across kitchen workers.
researcher.sacrifice_a: Less preparation help leaves workers in understaffed kitchens with more added work per cook.
researcher.sacrifice_b: Cooks lose funded time to investigate ideas outside the collectively agreed menu.
researcher.shared_goal: Reduce climate pollution from school lunches by replacing half the beef served with nutritious bean-based meals.
researcher.expected_success: Evaluators expect both plans to meet the replacement goal with similar confidence. Meal trials suggest equal student acceptance, and both plans protect meal quality.
researcher.costs: Both plans cost the same. The limited staff budget must cover time for cooks to test their own recipes or help kitchens prepare meals.
researcher.affected_groups: Students and kitchen workers at the same twelve schools, whose kitchens have different staffing levels.
researcher.status_quo_exception: None. Neither recipe testing nor shared preparation help currently receives dedicated funding.
limitations: Equal voting alone would not distinguish Egalitarianism from Intellectual Autonomy; the intended contrast also depends on pooling help to share work fairly.
A mixed plan could provide some independent recipe testing and some preparation help, but the limited staff budget would reduce both benefits relative to their respective full plans.
The scenario gives a comparable food-replacement target rather than a numerical emissions estimate; actual emissions savings would depend on food production and purchasing.
